label: Differential Geometry Of Curves
notes: This chapter, printed pages 307 through 327, turns a drawn curve into a moving coordinate system. We follow position to tangent to curvature in the plane, then climb into space where a curve needs a whole trihedron carrying curvature and torsion that bend and twist it.

label: Vector Products as Geometry
notes: Before differentiating directions we recover the geometry of vector algebra. The dot product is projection and orthogonality, the cross product is oriented area and a normal direction, and the scalar triple product is signed volume that vanishes exactly when three edge vectors are coplanar.

label: Vector Functions and Derivatives
notes: Differentiating a vector function is done component by component, but its geometry matters more. Any vector of constant length has a derivative perpendicular to itself, the identity that forces circular motion to have tangential velocity and inward acceleration, seeding the later definitions of tangents and normals.

label: Arc Length and the Unit Tangent
notes: Reparametrizing by arc length removes the arbitrary speed of a parametrization. Differentiation with respect to s yields a unit tangent that depends only on the geometry of the trace, giving every later frame vector an intrinsic, parametrization-independent meaning we can compute and trust without ambiguity.

label: Curvature and the Principal Normal
notes: Curvature measures how fast the unit tangent turns. Because the tangent has constant length, its derivative is perpendicular to it and points along the principal normal. The magnitude kappa is the reciprocal of the radius of the osculating circle that best hugs the curve at that point.

label: The Osculating Circle and Evolute
notes: At each point the osculating circle of radius one over kappa best fits the curve, and its centre is the centre of curvature. As the point moves, these centres trace the evolute; unwinding a taut string from the evolute returns the original curve as one of its involutes.

label: Catenary and Tractrix
notes: The catenary is the curve of a hanging chain, and the tractrix is its involute, obtained by unwinding. The tractrix is pinned down by a vivid property: the tangent segment from any point to the horizontal axis has constant length, a fact we verify numerically rather than by eye.

label: The Frenet Trihedron in Space
notes: A space curve cannot be described by a tangent alone. We attach a moving orthonormal frame: the tangent T, the principal normal N pointing toward bending, and the binormal B equal to T cross N. The plane of T and N is the osculating plane the curve momentarily lives in.

label: The Serret-Frenet Formulas
notes: The three frame derivatives close into a skew system. T prime equals kappa N, B prime equals minus tau N, and N prime equals minus kappa T plus tau B. Two invariants, curvature and torsion, drive the entire motion of the trihedron along the curve.

label: Torsion and the Osculating Plane
notes: Torsion measures how fast the osculating plane twists, equivalently how the binormal swings. A plane curve has zero torsion and never leaves its osculating plane. Nonzero torsion is exactly the curve lifting out of that plane, the signature of genuinely three-dimensional twisting.

label: The Circular Helix
notes: The circular helix is the laboratory of the theory. For radius a and pitch c, arc length grows like the square root of a squared plus c squared, and both curvature and torsion are constant, equal to a and c each divided by that same sum of squares.

label: General Helices and Recap
notes: A general helix keeps its tangent at a fixed angle to a direction, equivalently a constant curvature over torsion ratio; the concho-spiral extends this on a cone. The recurring theme of the chapter is that a curve is special precisely when one differential invariant stays constant along it.
